newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican president tours volcano to calm locals.
newsitem.headline: Mexican president tours volcano to calm locals.

text.p: As Mexico's Popocatepetl volcano rumbled ominously, President Ernesto Zedillo on Thursday toured nearby villages and tried to calm frightened residents at risk from possible new eruptions.

Despite Zedillo's soothing words, the 17,887-foot (5,500-meter) volcano blew three giant plumes of hot ash four miles (six km) into the air -- its fourth consecutive day of violent activity following its largest eruption in 70 years on Monday.

Zedillo circled the smoking volcano, the sixth-tallest in North America, in a helicopter and visited scores of villages on the mountain's flanks that sit just a few miles (kilometers) from the mud and lava-filled crater.
More than half a million people live directly around the volcano, one of the world's most active and potentially deadly. Mexico City, with 18 million residents, lies just 33 miles (50 km) away.

The Mexican leader played down the risk of a major eruption, but assured residents that officials had drawn up a massive evacuation plan involving up to 14,000 army troops and thousands of emergency vehicles and shelters just in case.

"Fortunately, scientists tell me it is unlikely we will have a major eruption; they have studied this and they think a serious incident is unlikely," said Zedillo, dressed in jeans and a leather jacket to ward off the volcano's high-altitude chill.

Disaster relief officials went on high alert on Monday when the volcano suddenly exploded, sending burning rocks flying through the air and a huge cloud of ash across much of central Mexico. It was the largest burst since the volcano sprang to life in December 1994 after decades of silence.
"I want you all to know that since December 1994 we have been preparing for whatever may happen," Zedillo told villagers.

Authorities temporarily evacuated several hundred residents of the nearby municipality of Santiago Xalitzintla from their homes late on Wednesday after a series of volcanic explosions caused a mudslide.
The residents returned to their homes on Thursday, but despite Zedillo's assurances many still feared the government had not done enough to ensure their safety.
"We don't know which way to go if there is an eruption, we have no telephone here, and the roads are lousy," an unidentified woman told Mexico City's Radio Red during the president's visit.

And although Zedillo arrived in the area by helicopter, journalists visiting by car said many of the area's roads were impassable because of recent rains. Televisa television network showed images of a yard (metre)-wide and deep crack in the road which serves as the main evacuation route from Santiago Xalitzintla.
Interior Minister Emilio Chuayfett said Sunday's key mid-term elections would take place in the area despite the threat posed by the volcano.
